claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure comprising dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Room-temperature ductility in the starting alloy is limited by dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar boundaries.
Controlled hot deformation followed immediately by rapid annealing will refine the lamellar colony interfaces.
Hot deformation followed by rapid annealing will promote in situ formation of nanoscale secondary precipitates.
The nanoscale secondary precipitates will form preferentially along internal lamellar interfaces.
Elevated-temperature deformation will activate dynamic recovery mechanisms.
Rapid annealing will freeze in the refined microstructure.
Rapid annealing after hot deformation will facilitate controlled nucleation of precipitates along lamellar interfaces.
Interface precipitates will modify the barrier characteristics of lamellar boundaries.
The precipitates will act as distributed sites for dislocation absorption or transmission.
The modified interfaces will promote more homogeneous dislocation movement across lamellar boundaries.
More homogeneous dislocation movement will reduce dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations.
Reducing local stress concentrations will mitigate microcrack nucleation and catastrophic damage during straining.
The treatment will increase room-temperature tensile elongation by more than 20% relative to the untreated material.
The treatment will maintain or increase strength relative to the untreated material.
Unwanted grain coarsening or misdistribution of secondary phases could prevent the proposed performance improvement.
The predicted improvement applies to room-temperature uniaxial tensile loading.
The predicted improvement may not generalize to high-strain-rate or high-temperature conditions.
